pr_title: Work around for ARM64 atomics bug
pr_body:
Avoid that by using ATOMIC_FALLBACKS for now.

Fixes: #26875
pr_comments: This is really a huge hammer. :cry:

What does broken mean here? Do you mean:
1. Arm64 atomics (or, more accurately, $compiler atomics on Arm64) do not correctly implement the C11/C++11 memory model?
2. Arm64 atomics (or, more accurately, $compiler atomics on Arm64) do implement the C11/C++11 memory model, but OpenSSL's RCU implementation requires more guarantees than the language provides?

If (1), that sounds like a compiler bug. Which compiler and have you filed a bug with the compiler?

If (2), that sounds like an OpenSSL bug that would impact potentially more than Arm64. If the compiler believes it is responsible for providing interface A and you need interface B, then you can't be sure that it does what you want on _any_ architecture.

The issue is still under investigation, but it seems to be caused by this code:
https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/d3b6b81eab48c1b8ed4075a1818692f640fea999/crypto/threads_pthread.c#L277-L285
which is translated into that
```
1001060d0: 91009289    	add	x9, x20, #36
1001060d4: b8bfc12b    	ldapr	w11, [x9]
1001060d8: f9400e89    	ldr	x9, [x20, #24]
1001060dc: 8b2b4d2c    	add	x12, x9, w11, uxtw #3
1001060e0: 52800029    	mov	w9, #1
1001060e4: f8a9018c    	ldadda	x9, x12, [x12]
1001060e8: b940268c    	ldr	w12, [x20, #36]
1001060ec: 6b0c017f    	cmp	w11, w12
1001060f0: 540001c0    	b.eq	0x100106128 <_ossl_rcu_read_lock+0x1cc>
```
this seems to behave is if the `ldr w12,[x20, #36]` uses a cached value in some cases,
and the increment of that use count is missed by the other CPU at the same time.
More background is in #26919 and #26898
Compiler: both clang and gcc seem to be affected.

So option 3) is that the CPU does not implement the atomics as documented.

And I'm not sure it's 1) or 3).

Ah true, it could be the CPU. But either (1) or (3) would require a mishap in some now fairly widespread systems, so that would be concerning / a little less likely than (2).

I'm still trying to understand this code, but you're trying to pick up the update to `reader_idx` with an acquiring fetch-add on `users`? What releasing store on `users` is that meant to match with? I see `update_qp` writes to `reader_idx`, so I'm guessing that's the update? I see that's called from `ossl_synchronize_rcu`, but that doesn't do a releasing store on `users`. The only releasing store I see is the fetch-sub in `ossl_rcu_read_unlock`.
I see there's also an acquiring load of `reader_idx`, but all stores are relaxed.

Checked with some folks who understand atomics much better than me, and they confirmed my understanding: if you're doing acquiring loads on some atomic without any releasing stores on _that same atomic_, the acquire isn't actually doing anything in the C11/C++11 memory model. (Particular compilers on particular architectures may happen to lower your code into machine code that introduces more happens-before edges, but to avoid problems like these, OpenSSL's code needs to be correct under the rules of that memory model.)

That means this comment is wrong:
https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/d3b6b81eab48c1b8ed4075a1818692f640fea999/crypto/threads_pthread.c#L476

I suspect you all need to dramatically strengthen the requirements on `reader_idx` accesses. Without synchronizing on that, none of the synchronizations on `users` would even hit the same atomic. At minimum, ISTM the `update_qp` write needs to be a releasing store. That way you have a happens-before chain from the sequence of `ossl_synchronize_rcu` calls that cleaned up and the cycled back around to your QP, down to the acquiring load on `get_hold_current_qp`.

I'm not sure if that is the only OpenSSL bug here (I'm far from an atomics expert), but it does seem to be one of them.

Hi @davidben 

get_hold_current_qp does

first read the reader_idx
then an acquire barrier so following read has to happen now
then add one to the users[idx]
again an acquire barrier so following read has to happen now
and then check if reader_idx is still same
if yes we have the read-lock
otherwise it was just a try-lock
release that, and try again.

and update_qp does
store a new value to reader_idx, do it simply relaxed,
the following pthread_mutex_unlock does the release barrier
then follows a pthread_mutex_lock which does an acquire barrier <- __this is super important
as otherwise on ppc64le the first atomic load can happen _before_ the release barrier above__
then loop as long as the atomic_load on the users[old_idx] is != 0

@bernd-edlinger I'm saying you all are *under*synchronized, not *over*synchronized. AIUI, those acquires only turn into happens-before edges across threads if they observe releasing stores to the _same_ atomic.
https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/atomic/memory_order#Release-Acquire_ordering
https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/atomic/memory_order#Synchronizes_with
https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/atomic/memory_order#Release-Acquire_ordering

> I suspect you all need to dramatically strengthen the requirements on reader_idx accesses. Without synchronizing on that, none of the synchronizations on users would even hit the same atomic. At minimum, ISTM the update_qp write needs to be a releasing store. That way you have a happens-before chain from the sequence of ossl_synchronize_rcu calls that cleaned up and the cycled back around to your QP, down to the acquiring load on get_hold_current_qp.

as the comment says this is supposed to synchronize with the ossl_rcu_read_unlock, which happens before and
does the RELEASE.
there is also https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/atomic/atomic_thread_fence

> as the comment says this is supposed to synchronize with the ossl_rcu_read_unlock, which happens before and
does the RELEASE.

`ossl_rcu_read_unlock` indeed has a releasing store on `users`. That means `ossl_rcu_read_unlock` happens-before [this load](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/d3b6b81eab48c1b8ed4075a1818692f640fea999/crypto/threads_pthread.c#L479) in `ossl_synchronize_rcu` call. This makes sense to me. You want to make sure the reader has unlocked before you retire the QP that uses it.

But that doesn't seem sufficient. The QP slots are looped around and reused. When some _other_ thread calls `ossl_rcu_read_lock`, it will take a lock on that QP, right? I assume that lock must happen-after retiring the previous incarnation of that QP? I do not see any synchronization in OpenSSL that ensures this.

My suggestion was to turn [this store](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/d3b6b81eab48c1b8ed4075a1818692f640fea999/crypto/threads_pthread.c#L408-L409) into release instead of relaxed, so that can synchronize with your acquiring read. Though I'm not sure if that is sufficient. I don't fully understand yet what this code is trying to do.  But, whatever the intended synchronization, something seems to be wrong in this code because [this acquire](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/d3b6b81eab48c1b8ed4075a1818692f640fea999/crypto/threads_pthread.c#L277) has no corresponding releasing store.

It's also worth keeping in mind that all this complexity and risk to OpenSSL applications is because OpenSSL 3.x went with a very mutation-heavy implementation of the OpenSSL providers idea. I think other issues have covered how more straightforwardly performant architectures could have achieved the same pluggability goals without all these problems.

The intent is that on each call to ossl_synchronize_rcu, the update_qp call has to block on the write side until such time as the "next" qp is available for use.  We do that by ensuring that the writers_alloced count is never less than 2 (see update_qp).  Because we retire them in the that update_qp issues them in, the "next" qp should always be available for a reader to use.

I see David's point here. This suggests https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/_005f_005fatomic-Builtins.html `_ATOMIC_RELAXED` is not what we want. If I understand things right we perform a store operation to `&lock->reader_idx`, so `_ATOMIC_RLEASE` is what we want, to pair the operation with `get_hold_current_qp()` where load happens.

https://developer.arm.com/documentation/102336/0100/Load-Acquire-and-Store-Release-instructions
says
```
The Shareability domain defines which Observers the ordering imposed by these instructions extend to.
The Shareability domain for a Load-Acquire and Store-Release is defined by the Shareability domain of
the address that is being accessed by the instruction. For example, if PE0 and PE1 are not in the same
Inner Shareable domain, then it would be architecturally permitted for PE1 to observe the memory
location at X3 updated before the memory location X1 is updated if X3 was defined as Inner Shareable.
This is shown in the following code:
```

the way I understand the paragraph is that `atomic_thread_fence()` done on behalf of mutex unlock does not count here because this fence operation is associated with mutex object address. So this fence works for all threads which lock/unlock mutex. However the atomic store operation here works on different address (&lock->qp_group[qp_idx].users). The thread which executes `get_hold_current_qp()` does not manipulate the address of mutex (observe the address) it is just modifying &lock->qp_group[qp_idx].users address. So therefore I think we need _ATOMIC_RELEASE in `update_qp()`.

For _ATOMIC_RELEASE the compiler emits `stlr w8, [x9]` instruction here. this `stlr` here is paired with `ldadda w8, [x8]` instruction in `get_hold_current_qp()` emitted on behalf of `ATOMIC_ADD_FETCH(&lock->qp_group[qp_idx].users, (uint64_t)1, _ATOMIC_ACQUIRE);`

This is at least my understanding (I admit I might still be missing lot of details here).

Do I feel right we can agree on the change in this PR goes in wrong direction? Can we close this PR then? thanks.

> the way I understand the paragraph is that `atomic_thread_fence()` done on behalf of mutex unlock does not count here because this fence operation is associated with mutex object address.

Does a mutex use a fence, or just an atomic release? A fence is without an associated atomic operation, where I expect a mutex to do an atomic operation.

@Sashan this mixes things up now.

A Shareability domain appears to be a concept where a system has a memory map,
where certain regions may be shared with certain CPU cores.
```
Armv8.1-A adds support for Limited Ordering Regions (LORegions). LORegions allow large
systems to perform special Load-Acquire (LDLAR) and Store-Release (STLLR) instructions
that provide order between the memory accesses only to a specified region of the Physical
Address (PA) map.

LORegions avoid the need to take large performance hits when waiting for a memory access, to
any location in the memory map, to be observed by all Observers in the same Shareability domain
as the initiating PE.
```
> For _ATOMIC_RELEASE the compiler emits `stlr w8, [x9]` instruction here. this `stlr` here is paired with `ldadda w8, [x8]` instruction

That is not correct, the address in the `stlr` is the the address of `reader_idx`, while the address
in the `ldadda` is the address of `qp_group[qp_idx]` thus they are not paired.

Furthermore we do not really use C11 atomics, but the GNU C atomic builtin functions,
so `__atomic_load_n`, `__atomic_store_n` etc.

</snip>
> 
> That is not correct, the address in the `stlr` is the the address of `reader_idx`, while the address in the `ldadda` is the address of `qp_group[qp_idx]` thus they are not paired.

yes you are right I've pasted wrong instruction there is `ldapr` which loads `reader_idx` right at the beginning of `get_hold_current_qp()`  using `ATOMIC_LOAD_N()`.

> 
> Furthermore we do not really use C11 atomics, but the GNU C atomic builtin functions, so `__atomic_load_n`, `__atomic_store_n` etc.

I'm compiling code on macOS with clang tool chain so the disassembly i'm looking at comes from clang.

so for what its worth this patch ran overnight on linux-arm64 and is at 12835 iterations, and no failures, but at a 10x performance slowdown
Closing this in favor of #27002

review_comments:
It would be nice if we had a comment in the code that pointed to what we think the break in atomics is here. 

FWIW, I just ran across this:
https://lists.infradead.org/pipermail/linux-arm-kernel/2014-February/229588.html

In trying to better understand the situation.  It seems to allude to the same problem you have been describing.  The kernel solved it by re-implementing their atomics for arm as full barriers

Yeah, this somehow matches to my theory how the acquire barrier might be in the middle of the atomic_add:
https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/26919#issuecomment-2691275845
but here we have a single atomic instruction, and the magnitude of the probability of that effect that I had
observed on my MACOS M1 experiments makes me wonder if there is a barrier at all.

Some context here is that the Linux kernel uses a different memory model from the standard C11 one.
https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2020/p0124r7.html
